name: Lacrosse ball / massage gun

lead: A lacrosse ball pressed against a wall or floor, or a handheld massage gun, is used to release tight chest, neck, upper-back and hip muscles linked to rounded shoulders and slouching. The goal is an easier, more upright posture.

Pressure or percussion eases muscle tension and improves range of motion, which makes it simpler to hold a better position. Studies cover recovery, soreness and mobility. Some forum users also use massage guns on the face for symmetry or in bonesmashing; no published work covers those uses.

paras: People use them for a few minutes on tight areas before or after training or at the end of a day, often alongside stretching and strengthening for the posture muscles. Effects on soreness and mobility are usually felt within a session.

A case report links massage gun use to rhabdomyolysis. Bruising and nerve irritation can follow heavy pressure, and people on blood thinners or with circulation problems are usually advised to be careful. Both are sold as consumer wellness devices.

angle.text: Lacrosse balls and massage guns release tight chest, neck and back muscles tied to rounded posture, which makes an upright stance easier to hold. Trials have studied them for recovery and mobility.

lead: A lacrosse ball is a firm rubber ball used for self-massage against a wall or floor, and a massage gun is a handheld battery-powered percussive device that delivers rapid pulses, commonly 20 to 60 Hz, through interchangeable heads. Both are used for muscle tension, soreness and trigger-point release.[1]

Research on percussive massage is described as limited. Randomized and crossover studies have examined recovery, range of motion and pain, and a case report documented rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use.[2][3][4] On looksmax.org, users also discuss massage guns in connection with bonesmashing, a practice with no published support.[5][6]

paras: Electric percussive massagers were patented in the mid-twentieth century and sold mostly to physiotherapists and chiropractors until the 2010s. Consumer models spread after Theragun, developed by chiropractor Jason Wersland, and Hyperice's Hypervolt in 2018, with social media and the COVID-19 period boosting sales.[1]

A 5-minute massage gun application was tested for perceptual and physical recovery in active adults, in a study whose authors called the devices new and under-researched.[2] A trial examined percussive massage with and without heat on calf muscle properties.[7] A self-myofascial release study of the superficial back line reported improved sit-and-reach distance.[8] A randomized trial tested local vibration therapy in cervical disc herniation for pain and function.[4] A case report described using a lacrosse ball with compression tack and flossing for adolescent Achilles tendinopathy.[9] No studies found testing either tool for facial structure or bone changes.
A 2021 case report in Physical Therapy described rhabdomyolysis after massage gun use.[3] Forum users note the heads could harm the eye area at high settings.[6]
Users on looksmax.org ask whether bonesmashing combined with a massage gun has any effect, and some say the soft attachments are unlikely to change bone but may help asymmetry.[5][6]

lore.intro: Massage guns appear in looksmaxxing threads mainly alongside bonesmashing and muscle-tension discussions.[5][6]
